title: Joshua 14:1–5
context: Joshua 14 begins the account of the western allotments. Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the tribal heads distribute the land by lot, as God commanded through Moses, while the narrative recalls that the eastern tribes already have their land and that Levi receives towns rather than territory. Joseph counts as two tribes, keeping twelve landed tribes. Both traditions read these verses as shared ground about orderly obedience and God’s providence in the lot.

verses.text: These are the inheritances which the children of Israel took in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar the priest, Joshua the son of Nun, and the heads of the fathers’ houses of the tribes of the children of Israel, distributed to them,
verses.arminianNotes:
These are the inheritances in Canaan distributed by Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the tribal heads. Leadership is shared between priest, leader, and elders.

Arminian readers see a community process carried out under God’s direction, as Numbers 34:16–29 had arranged.
verses.reformedNotes:
Eleazar is named first, perhaps reflecting the role of the priest with the lot. The distribution is both sacred and civic.

Reformed readers see God’s gift administered through appointed leaders. Both traditions read this as shared ground about orderly, God-directed stewardship.

verses.text: by the lot of their inheritance, as the LORD commanded by Moses, for the nine tribes, and for the half-tribe.
verses.arminianNotes:
The land is distributed by lot, as the LORD commanded through Moses, to the nine and a half tribes. The lot leaves the outcome with God.

Arminian readers see fairness in a method that no tribe could manipulate.
verses.reformedNotes:
The lot expresses trust that God decides each portion. Proverbs 16:33 states the same conviction.

Reformed readers see God’s providence governing the allotment. Both traditions agree that the lot here is God’s appointed means and read this as shared ground, with differing emphasis on how providence works.

verses.text: For Moses had given the inheritance of the two tribes and the half-tribe beyond the Jordan; but to the Levites he gave no inheritance among them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Moses had already given the two and a half eastern tribes their land, and the Levites received none among them. The narrative ties east and west together.

Arminian readers see continuity with the arrangements made in Numbers 32 and 35.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse recalls chapter 13. The Levites’ special status is stated again.

Reformed readers see the consistency of God’s instructions across the books. Both traditions read this as shared ground, with Levi’s lack of land pointing to its calling to serve the LORD among all the tribes.

verses.text: For the children of Joseph were two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim. They gave no portion to the Levites in the land, except cities to dwell in, with their pasture lands for their livestock and for their property.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joseph’s descendants formed two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim, and the Levites received only towns with pasture lands. This keeps the number of landed tribes at twelve.

Arminian readers see God’s arrangement balancing the tribes fairly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Joseph’s double portion reflects Jacob’s blessing in Genesis 48:5. Levi’s cities are those described in Numbers 35.

Reformed readers see earlier promises shaping later structures. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the coherence of God’s plan for Israel.

verses.text: The children of Israel did as the LORD commanded Moses, and they divided the land.
verses.arminianNotes:
Israel did as the LORD commanded Moses and divided the land. Obedience is affirmed.

Arminian readers see a faithful response that contrasts with the failures noted in 13:13. Obedience and failure both appear honestly in the record.
verses.reformedNotes:
The summary emphasizes conformity to God’s command. The distribution follows the instructions given in Numbers.

Reformed readers see God’s word carried out by his people. Both traditions read this as shared ground and as an introduction to the individual allotments that begin with Caleb’s request.
